name: Endermologie / LPG

lead: Endermologie, made by the French company LPG, is a motorised roller-and-suction massage treatment used to soften the look of cellulite and improve body contour.

The device pulls and rolls the skin with suction and rollers, a mechanical massage of the tissue beneath. Small studies of tens to a hundred or so women, including 33 and 118 participants, assessed cellulite grade and body measurements after about 15 sessions over several weeks. It is also used for lymphedema alongside compression.

paras: It is a course of roughly 15 sessions, around twice weekly, in a clinic or spa.
The sources describe it as FDA-approved as a massage system and do not detail adverse events. Larger controlled studies were not found among them.

angle.text: It is used to soften the look of cellulite and improve body contour: machine massage works the skin and tissue beneath, leaving smoother texture. Small studies report contour and texture changes, and large controlled evidence is limited.

lead: Endermologie, produced by the French company LPG, is a machine-assisted massage system that rolls the skin between motorised rollers while applying suction, intended to improve the look of cellulite and body contour.[1] It was originally developed in the late 1970s in France to soften scars and standardise physical therapy, and clinicians then noticed changes in contour and skin texture in treated patients.[1]

Small clinical studies have evaluated it. One study of 33 women with cellulite gave 15 sessions twice weekly, and another of 118 women used a similar schedule; both assessed cellulite grade and body measurements.[2][3] These papers describe the device as FDA-approved as a massage system, and the 2009 authors described it as lacking clinical study at that point.[2][3]
It has also been explored for lymphedema in combination with compression bandaging, a medical rather than cosmetic use.[4][5]
infobox: Mechanical rolling and suction massage device
Described as FDA-approved as a massage system

paras: The system applies positive-pressure rolling together with negative pressure to skin and subcutaneous tissue.[1] A 1998 report states it was developed in France in the late 1970s for scars and physical therapy, and that its body-contour use followed from observed effects of treatment.[1] Wikipedia's cellulite article lists mechanical suction and massage among non-invasive options and notes that cellulite can be resistant to many treatments.[6]

A 1998 outcome study reported one-year results of treatment for body contouring.[1] A 2009 study treated 33 healthy women with grade 1 to 3 cellulite twice weekly for 15 sessions, assessing photographs and circumference measurements.[2] A 2013 study enrolled 118 women on the same schedule and evaluated cellulite grade, safety and slimming.[3] The abstracts available do not allow a detailed account of effect sizes.

In lymphedema, a 2007 report presented two protocols combining the system with compression bandaging in women with secondary arm lymphedema, a phase II randomised trial protocol was published in 2019 for breast cancer related lymphedema, and a registered trial of a treatment pathway for breast cancer related lymphoedema exists.[4][5][7]
